newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT-Lagging small caps draw heightened concern.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Lagging small caps draw heightened concern.

text.p: With each week this year, the U.S. stock market has seen one class of equities after another fall behind an elite corps of large cap names whose relentless run into record territory has kept alive the bull market.

Now, amid undeniable evidence that investors largely shunned small caps during the massive January market cash influx, analysts are even less hopeful the Dow's ascent through 7000 will translate into a broad rally.
And, as a consequence, an increasing number see troubled times ahead.
Since December 31, 1996, the Dow Jones Industrial Average .DJI has risen 9.6 percent, just a trace behind the 10.2 percent advance staged by the S&P 500 index .SPX.

Over the same period, the Nasdaq Composite index .IXIC has risen 5.8 percent -- trailing off lately on weakness in the networking sector -- the S&P Midcap 400 .SPM has climbed 5.3 percent and the Russell 2000 small cap index .RUT has eked out a lowly 2.1 percent gain.

"We need the broader market to expand and that's not happening," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "We've had a lack of participation from the secondary and third-tier stocks."
Others are also counselling caution, although several strategists noted that as the large cap rally has picked up steam, their advice has often fallen on deaf ears.
"I think the overall picture for small caps is all part of a big market top and I'm suggesting you go into cash," said John Wosczyna, market strategist at Roney & Co.

Wosczyna said he would not be surprised by a Dow correction of 25 to 30 percent this year -- certainly reason for a sizable cash position. But even so, he said, "90 percent of my portfolio managers say, 'I can't hold cash.'"

Cardillo did boost cash in his asset allocation model, albeit to a very modest five percent position. The move, which drew his stocks position down to 65 percent from 70 percent with the balance in bonds, is ahead of what he expects could be a five to eight percent Dow correction starting in March.
"It doesn't change my bullish posture from a fundamental perspective but I think we could be in for a rocky period," he said. "March and April are traditionally weak months."
Even after such a fall, the Dow's rise for the year would roughly match the Russell's, noteworthy because the traditional January rally has long been a small cap feature.

"The Russell continues to lag and frankly, that's been surprising," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co. "You're seeing a more cautious market with money flowing to the Merck's and the Coke's."

The flight to liquidity has been a hallmark of the large cap rally, which gained vigor after last July's sell-off. Lately, however, the rally has begun fueling itself, sparking interest in S&P 500 index funds, for example.
"The mentality of this market is very much like what happened to low-priced stocks in 1983 and 1993," Wosczyna said. "People are just bidding them up and bidding them up."
Even so, few analysts expressed a bleak outlook on the market. Rather, most remain -- yes -- cautious.
"The market is still technically healthy," Green said. "The only concern is the narrow leadership. At this point, the worst case downside scenario is 6600 (on the Dow)."
